old: It honors the man who founded a city's police force, worn as a nickname rather than a title.
The word is just a friendly short form of a common first name, given to the officers of that force.
Think of the name behind it — Robert — shortened the way friends might call someone at home.
clues: This affectionate British nickname for a kind of uniformed public servant began as the everyday, familiar form of one particular man's first name.
A police officer, especially one walking the beat, warmer and more old-fashioned than 'cop'. It first meant only London's officers, then spread to any in Britain.
It honors Sir Robert Peel, who established London's police force, and is simply the familiar form of Robert, as in the picture of one in a tall helmet.
